subject: Biotechnology
title: Enzymes: Biological Catalysts
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Enzymes: Biological Catalysts.

hook.text: Without enzymes, digesting a meal would take 2.3 billion years — enzymes speed reactions a millionfold.

buildup.text: Enzymes are proteins that lower the energy barrier of chemical reactions — catalysts made by cells.

discovery.text: Each enzyme fits its substrate like a lock and key — exquisite specificity with no wasted effort.

twist.text: Enzymes work at body temperature and neutral pH — industrial catalysts often need extreme heat and pressure.

climax.text: Biotech uses enzymes in everything from laundry detergent to DNA sequencing — nature's catalysts, everywhere.

punchline.text: Life runs on enzymes — biotech puts them to work outside the body.

quiz.question: Why are enzymes preferred over industrial catalysts in many applications?
options: Enzymes are always cheaper to produce than chemical catalysts
Enzymes work at mild temperatures with high specificity

details.summary: Enzymes are protein catalysts that accelerate biological reactions by millions of times without being consumed. Each enzyme has a specific active site that fits particular substrates like a lock and key, enabling the precise chemical transformations that sustain all life.
details.whyItMatters: Enzymes are the workhorses of biotechnology. Industrial processes use them in detergents, food production, and pharmaceutical synthesis. Engineering better enzymes through directed evolution is a major focus of modern biotechnology.
takeaways: Enzymes lower activation energy to speed reactions by factors of millions
Substrate specificity arises from the shape of the enzyme's active site
Industrial enzymes are a multi-billion dollar global market

faq.question: Why are enzymes so important in biotechnology?
faq.answer: Enzymes enable precise chemical transformations under mild conditions that would require harsh chemicals, high temperatures, or high pressures using conventional chemistry. They are essential tools for everything from PCR diagnostics to biofuel production.

faq.question: Can enzymes be engineered to do things they do not do naturally?
faq.answer: Yes. Directed evolution applies rounds of random mutation and selection to create enzymes with new functions. Rational design uses structural knowledge to modify active sites. These approaches have produced enzymes catalyzing reactions never seen in nature.
